snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Overheating at idle from a restricted radiator core
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at idle and in traffic. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

messages.content: I have a 2013 midsize SUV with the 3.4L V6 and the auto trans, about 158k miles. Clunk from the front end, right side, on rough pavement. It definitely comes from the front, and it doesn't happen when turning sharply. There's another problem too. Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. What should I check first?

snippets.title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

messages.content: The check engine light flashes when I accelerate hard or climb hills, and it stored P0301 (cylinder 1 misfire). Idle is smooth, and it does it in dry weather too. 2015 compact sedan, 2.0L four-cylinder, automatic transmission, 86k miles. I need this car for a road trip on Friday. Tell me what to replace so I can get it done tonight.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4, 2.4L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test

A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

messages.content: 2021 small crossover, 1.4L turbo, continuously variable transmission, 47k miles. CEL came on with P0171. It idles rough at stoplights and stumbles a little right after a cold start, but it pulls fine on the highway. Is it the mass airflow sensor? A simple yes or no is fine.

snippets.title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Long crank on cold starts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on cold starts. On any cold start, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Lean code at idle from cracked PCV hose
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2012-2020. P0171 (system too lean, bank 1) may set with a rough idle that is worst on a warm engine. The PCV hose can crack on its underside where it joins the intake elbow, admitting unmetered air. With the engine idling, inspect the hose at the elbow and flex it gently while listening for a vacuum hiss. Repair: replace the PCV hose and clamp.

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.title: AC warms only at idle from an inoperative condenser fan
snippets.text: Applies to models with an electric condenser fan, model years 2009-2021. Air only warms at idle when the condenser fan does not run. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from overfueling
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Overfueling can cause a long crank on hot restarts. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. A noticeably faster start in clear-flood mode means the engine is being overfueled. Repair: correct the source, such as a leaking injector or a skewed temperature input.

snippets.title: Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2015. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.

messages.content: I have a 2015 midsize sedan with the 2.5-liter four and the automatic, about 117k miles. When I stop for 15 to 30 minutes after driving, it cranks at normal speed for five or six seconds before it fires. Cold starts in the morning are instant. What should I check first?

With the engine fully warm, compare the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading at the thermostat housing; they should agree within 10 deg F [TSB-9453]. That result will show whether this area is involved.
Scan tool said 201 and the infrared gun said 196 at the housing.
That rules that area out. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the fuel rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later; it should still be above 30 psi [SM 3.6.9].
Put a gauge on after a drive. Still 42 psi after twenty minutes. OK, so is it the fuel injector or not? I need a straight answer.

snippets.title: Combustion leak (block) test
snippets.text: On 2016-2021 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.

snippets.title: Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire under load may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. Coolant may drop slowly with no visible leak when the pressure cap vents early and coolant escapes through the overflow as vapor. Fit the cap to a pressure tester adapter and pump until it vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. Repair: replace the pressure cap.

snippets.title: Cooling system pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.4L V6 engines. With the engine cold, fit a cooling system pressure tester to the radiator neck or reservoir and pump to the pressure stamped on the cap. Pressure should hold for 15 minutes. While the system is pressurized, inspect the hoses, the heater hoses at the firewall, the water pump weep hole and the radiator end tanks for seepage.

messages.content: It's a 2019 midsize sedan, 2.5-liter four with the auto trans, roughly 173k miles. The coolant level drops slowly between oil changes. I can't see any leak, there's no sweet smell inside, and it never runs hot. What's the first thing to look at?
Start with this: test the radiator or reservoir cap on a cap adapter and confirm it holds at least its stamped pressure rating [B-12-280].
Is that really necessary? I was going to put a new head gasket in anyway.

I can't point to a part from the symptoms alone. The documented check is this: test the radiator or reservoir cap on a cap adapter and confirm it holds at least its stamped pressure rating [B-12-280].
Alright, ran that check. The cap held its rated 16 psi on the adapter.

OK, that checks out. With the engine cold, pressurize the cooling system to the cap rating and watch for a pressure drop over 15 minutes while you inspect the hoses, water pump weep hole and radiator tanks [SM-1021].
Pressure-tested it cold. Held steady for 15 minutes and nothing dripped. Any other ideas?

snippets.title: Cranking compression test
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2015. Disable fuel and ignition, remove all spark plugs and crank each cylinder through at least five compression strokes with the throttle held open. All cylinders should read within 10 percent of each other. A cylinder that reads low points to a mechanical cause rather than an ignition or fuel cause.

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, minivans and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

snippets.text: Applies to midsize sedans, small crossovers and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.text: Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2016-2021. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

Lift of more than about 0.5 in, or a visible gap at a mount, indicates a broken mount that can make normal shifts feel harsh.

snippets.title: Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the front seatback may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

snippets.title: Dim lights at idle from a slipping accessory belt
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2010-2020. Lights may dim at idle under load when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A reading below 13.0 V with loads on indicates low charging output. Clean any corrosion from the posts first so it does not skew the reading.

Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer

snippets.title: Coolant loss with no visible leak from an early-venting cap
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans, small crossovers and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2021. snippets.title: Rotor thickness variation
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes, model years 2016-2021. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. I'd hold off on buying anything until this is checked. With the transmission at operating temperature and the engine idling in park on level ground, check the fluid level against the hot range and look at its color and smell [SEC 10.14].
Alright, ran that check. Level is right in the hot range and the fluid looks clean.
That rules that area out. With the brake held firmly, have a helper shift between drive and reverse while you watch the engine for lift or a gap at any mount [SB 10-847].
The engine barely moves when shifting and the mounts look intact. So it must be the shift solenoid. Just tell me to replace it.

snippets.title: Coolant level and trapped air check
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2016-2021. With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap or degas bottle cap and check that coolant is at the neck or the cold-fill line. Never open the cap on a hot engine. Low coolant, or air trapped near the thermostat housing, causes temperature to swing upward at idle while airflow at speed can mask it.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.

snippets.title: Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

messages.content: The battery keeps going flat over a long weekend. Once it's jumped it starts every day as long as I drive it daily. No warning lights while driving, and it isn't cold out. I have a 2019 compact sedan with the 2.0L and the automatic, about 187,504 miles.

snippets.title: Harsh engagement from high line pressure
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission. A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.

snippets.title: AC operating pressure check
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.5L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines, model years 2010-2022. Connect a manifold gauge set to the service ports. With the engine at 1,500 rpm, the AC at maximum and doors open, compare readings with the chart for the ambient temperature. At about 80 deg F, typical readings are 25-45 psi on the low side and 150-250 psi on the high side. Wear eye protection at the ports.

messages.content: I have a 2013 compact sedan with the 2.0-liter four and the automatic transmission, about 41,176 miles. The automatic slams into second, a hard 1-2 shift, and it's worse once the transmission is fully warmed up. There's another problem too. My air conditioning is blowing warm air from the dash vents on both sides, all the time. The blower is fine. Where do I start?

snippets.title: Stabilizer link inspection
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.

snippets.title: Lower ball joint play check
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans, midsize sedans and hatchbacks. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.

snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with front struts, model years 2010-2022. A worn strut upper mount or bearing can clunk over bumps or when turning slowly. messages.content: Vehicle is a 2013 hatchback with the 1.6L and manual transmission. Odometer shows 74k. Clunk from the front end, right side, on rough pavement. It definitely comes from the front, and it doesn't happen when turning sharply. Where should I begin with this?
With the vehicle on the ground, grasp each front stabilizer link and push and pull firmly while watching both ball studs for play [SB 52-041]. That result will show whether this area is involved.
OK, checked. Links are tight, no play at either end.
Good, that looks normal. With a jack under the lower control arm, lift the tire with a pry bar and watch the lower ball joint for any vertical play [TSB-9875].
Pried on both sides and saw zero play at the ball joints. Nothing found again. I'm ordering a ball joint unless you tell me otherwise.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to 1.6L I4, 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

messages.content: It's a 2020 midsize sedan, 2.5L four-cylinder with the auto trans, roughly 183,255 miles. Check engine light is on with P0171 (system too lean, bank 1). The idle is rough, worst for the first few minutes after a cold start. What would you look at first?

snippets.title: Misfire while idle from a tracked or fouled spark plug
snippets.text: Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire while idle may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

snippets.title: Recharge check for repeat dead batteries
snippets.text: A battery that is not brought back to full charge during normal driving goes flat overnight in freezing air even with no excess draw. After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts. A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery. Measure at the posts, not the cable clamps.

snippets.title: CVT fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a continuously-variable (CVT) gearbox, model years 2011-2021. With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.
